# StarPower Collective — full site text

StarPower Collective is an internet radio show from Harlem, New York, started in 2010, interviewing everyday people and well-known artists about the music that shaped their lives. Interviews play in rotation on Nu Soul Hwy Radio (https://starpowercollective.com). Founded by Derek B. (Power), Dano B. (SuperStar), Ron J. (Dast-One), Sid W. (Da Creator) and Keith H. (KV).


## About StarPower Collective
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/#story
It started in Harlem in 2010 with a crew, one mic and a simple belief: everyday people are Stars. StarPower Collective interviews the people who shape our lives about the music that shaped theirs: the neighbor, the teacher, the DJ, the grandmother who still knows every word. It has also welcomed legends like Kool Mo Dee, Kidd Creole, Don Blackman and Onaje Allan Gumbs. Each interview becomes a guest's own accolade, shared with family and friends. Some guests have since passed, and their interviews were their last recordings; those recordings were given to their families. Taglines: "Do you have StarPower? Sure, you do." "Every Life Has a Soundtrack." "Music is the shower of life!" "It takes a village to raise a radio."

## The Founding Five
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/#founders
- Derek B. ("Power"): grew up on 129th Street between Convent Avenue and St. Nicholas Terrace ("the Hill"). Came up with the idea for StarPower as a way to create "a better, loving space." Music is "the score, the soundtrack to our life."
- Dano B. ("SuperStar"): Derek's brother. Caught the DJ bug at ten in 1972 at his father's house parties; DJed lunchrooms and school dances at Norman Thomas High School. For Dano, StarPower is "a sanctuary, a haven."
- Ron J. ("Dast-One"): grew up on 152nd–153rd Street near the Jackie Robinson pool and the Polo Grounds. "Music is my life. Bottom line. Straight, no chaser."
- Sid W. ("Da Creator"): grew up on 127th Street; music is "the shower of life." Designer, educator, published poet and songwriter who builds StarPower's look and sound.
- Keith H. ("KV"): grew up on St. Nicholas Terrace, on Da Hill. For Keith, music is a time machine. Da Hill 4 Life.
Together they also founded Nu Soul Hwy Radio, Immoortal Souls and Psyba Village.

## The Village Speaks (listener testimonials)
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/#voices
- "Thanks for keepin' StarPower Collective alive. My disappointment is when I'm not here. True words, not a story." (Avon Ballard)
- "I say this each and every week… truly love what you gentlemen are doing! Big ups to the entire StarPower family!" (Almeta Miller)
- "May the Peace, Love and Positive Energy that was intended when my 'Brothers' created this space continue to shine with Force! Love you guys!" (Nikki Nicole Howard)
- "Ordinary folks sharing their life through music shows the ultimate human connection through music, lyrics and song! No other place like it on any of my lists!" (Pamela Phillips)
Listeners and past guests can share their own StarPower story through the form on the site.

## Immoortal Souls
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/#legacy
"Give Them Their Flowers While They're Here." Immoortal Souls (spelled with two o's) grew out of StarPower Collective after families said the recordings of guests who had passed became priceless. It captures a loved one's voice, stories and wisdom through guided conversations, protects photographs and family history, and creates a keepsake to pass down. Families can request a free Legacy Call on the site. Nothing is shared without the family's consent.

## Kool Mo Dee
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/interviews/kool-mo-dee/
Hip-hop pioneer and member of the Treacherous Three.

Kool Mo Dee helped write the early rules of hip-hop as a member of the Treacherous Three. On StarPower Collective, he went back further, to the records that shaped him before he ever picked up a mic.
One song stopped him cold: Michael Jackson's "Rock with You." He couldn't believe a single record could carry street credibility, win over pop radio and still work for hip-hop all at once. For a young Black boy, he said, it made anything feel possible.
His musical education started at home. His mother loved Dionne Warwick and Aretha Franklin, and she told him stories about Frankie Lymon and the Teenagers, singing the songs to him a cappella. Through the family he also heard Harry Belafonte, calypso, Miriam Makeba and African chants, music he felt long before he understood the words.
Kool Mo Dee is honest that he doesn't love all music. He loves the music he loves. But when a record hits, he says, it becomes a universal language, and the songs with something to say are the ones that stay with him.

Quotes:
- "I didn't love music. I love the music I loved." — Kool Mo Dee
- "It's like you can feel stuff and communicate without speech." — Kool Mo Dee

Playlist: Michael Jackson – "Rock with You"; Aretha Franklin; Dionne Warwick; Harry Belafonte – "Day-O"; Frankie Lymon and the Teenagers; Miriam Makeba

## Inspectah Deck
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/interviews/inspectah-deck/
MC and producer, member of the Wu-Tang Clan.

Inspectah Deck is known worldwide as one of the sharpest MCs in the Wu-Tang Clan. On StarPower Collective, he talked about music the way most people never hear him talk about it: as therapy.
His earliest memories belong to his mother. She kept a stack of 45s with her initials written on every record so everyone knew whose they were, and she kept the house full of soul. Stephanie Mills was always in his head. As a kid in junior high he also played piano and violin, and he says he wants to get back to the keys.
Curtis Mayfield sits at the top of his list. Deck admires him as a Black man who wasn't afraid to be Black on record, and as an artist who let the beat ride for two minutes before the first lyric, putting you in a trance. He says he takes that same approach into his own rhymes.
He calls himself a child of the '70s, from Tarika Blue's "Dreamflower" to the soul records that later fed hip-hop's samples, and he still carries that era into his music.

Quotes:
- "I use music as therapy." — Inspectah Deck
- "He let the beat rock two minutes before he even brought the lyrics in. So you're already in a trance." — Inspectah Deck

Playlist: Curtis Mayfield – "Give Me Your Love"; Stephanie Mills; Tarika Blue – "Dreamflower"

## Onaje Allan Gumbs
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/interviews/onaje-allan-gumbs/
Jazz pianist, composer and arranger.

Pianist, composer and arranger Onaje Allan Gumbs saw music as something meant to heal and nourish. On StarPower Collective, he compared musicians to chefs: it starts with the heartbeat, then the melody, and his mission was to serve listeners every course in the world of sound.
He traced his first major break to drummer Norman Connors, who heard him and asked him to arrange music for a record. That assignment became the title track of Connors' album "Dark of Light," and the musicians on the session were jazz royalty. Connors was so impressed he encouraged Onaje to take the next step in his own career.
As a young listener, Onaje fell so hard for film scores that he wanted every record a composer made and to see every movie that composer scored. He also credited the late Dr. Billy Taylor, the pianist and educator he heard on the radio, as a big influence.

Quotes:
- "Music to me is an art form that I feel is meant to be used to heal and to nourish." — Onaje Allan Gumbs
- "We as musicians are very much like chefs." — Onaje Allan Gumbs

Playlist: Norman Connors – "Dark of Light"; Dr. Billy Taylor

## Don Blackman
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/interviews/don-blackman/
Keyboardist, singer and songwriter from Jamaica, Queens.

Keyboardist, singer and songwriter Don Blackman grew up in Jamaica, Queens, in a house where music lived on every floor. His mother, his aunt and several uncles played piano or saxophone. When his Pentecostal grandparents were home, it was gospel. When they left, he remembered, the first floor was jazz, the second floor was R&B and the basement was classical. That mix, he said, is why he could play so many styles authentically.
The first record he bought with his own money was James Brown's "Cold Sweat." His first concert, at 17, was saxophonist Charles McPherson with Sam Jones on bass and Louis Hayes on drums.
Funkadelic's "Knee Deep" holds a special story. He played it for hours at his cousin's house until his cousin begged him to stop. Later, at Funkadelic's show at the Apollo, the band recognized him, brought him in, and he ended up on stage playing "Knee Deep" with them.
Don also talked about Earth, Wind & Fire's "After the Love Has Gone," George Duke and Michael Jackson. For him, music was simply life.

Quotes:
- "Music is life. Music is emotion. Music is spiritual. Music is guidance. Music is heart." — Don Blackman
- "Music is universal." — Don Blackman

Playlist: Funkadelic – "Knee Deep"; James Brown – "Cold Sweat"; Earth, Wind & Fire – "After the Love Has Gone"; George Duke; Michael Jackson – "Another Part of Me"

## Reggie Reg
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/interviews/reggie-reg/
MC with the legendary Crash Crew.

Reggie Reg of the legendary Crash Crew told StarPower Collective how a group of friends from the same Harlem building turned into one of hip-hop's early crews.
Most of them had known each other since kindergarten. Two older DJs in the building, Mike and Dave, threw parties every other weekend, and at 15 and 16 Reggie and his friends helped carry the equipment down from the fourth floor and pack it up afterward. Eventually they asked to get down with them. Mike taught them to cut and mix, and within about a month they had a mixtape they were selling in junior high and high school.
By 1978 and 1979 the crew was building full routines and playing shows in the era of Sergio Valente jeans and Pro-Keds. They recorded with Mike and Dave for about three years before moving on.
Reggie's taste runs from upbeat break beats to Earth, Wind & Fire, whose music he says can lift you out of a low mood.

Quotes:
- "If you're in a little depressed mood, you put on some Earth, Wind & Fire, it can motivate you." — Reggie Reg

Playlist: Earth, Wind & Fire; Classic break beats

## Dennis Coffey
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/interviews/dennis-coffey/
Detroit guitarist, Motown session player and creator of "Scorpio".

Detroit guitarist Dennis Coffey played on more hits than most people could name. On StarPower Collective, he walked through a career that started at 15, when he played his first recording session, got paid $15 a song and heard himself on the radio two weeks later.
Music ran in the family. His mother played piano and sang big band standards, and she told him he could name every song on the radio at two or three years old. Cousins playing country music got him started on guitar, and he practiced up to eight hours a day in the summer before studying harmony and theory at Wayne State University.
At Motown he joined a producers' workshop, and a new wah-wah pedal a friend lent him became the sound of The Temptations' "Cloud Nine." He also used an Echoplex tape-echo machine on guitar. Sessions were cut live, one song an hour with no overdubs, and some of his best-known parts were made up on the spot.
His own record, "Scorpio," did nothing for its first year. Then dance clubs started playing it, and it went gold. He says it has been sampled more than 90 times. Dennis still values what Detroit taught him: it didn't matter what color you were, only whether you could play.

Quotes:
- "In Detroit, it didn't matter what color you were. It was just you could play or you couldn't play." — Dennis Coffey
- "We did one song an hour with no mistakes." — Dennis Coffey

Playlist: Dennis Coffey – "Scorpio"; The Temptations – "Cloud Nine"; Hank Williams; Jimmy Reed; B.B. King

## Josh Milan
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/interviews/josh-milan/
Singer, songwriter and producer from Fort Greene, Brooklyn.

Singer, songwriter and producer Josh Milan was born and raised in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. On StarPower Collective, he remembered a neighborhood that was poor but close, and said that togetherness is what he misses most.
His parents were church people, so gospel filled the house, while right outside the door the block was scratching and rapping. Anyone with two turntables and a mixer could rock a block party, and music was simply a way of life. When he first heard "The Message," he took it home and played it all night on his mother's stereo.
His first concert was a church choir day, and he still feels that same rush when he sees a show today, as he did recently at a Gregory Porter concert. He calls James Taylor a genius songwriter, praises bassist Derrick Hodge and names Quincy Jones as a lasting influence on his production.
For Josh, music is spiritual at its core.

Quotes:
- "When I hear music, I hear God." — Josh Milan
- "It was a lifestyle." — Josh Milan

Playlist: Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five – "The Message"; George Benson (produced by Quincy Jones); James Taylor; The Police; Derrick Hodge

## Boyd Jarvis
URL: https://starpowercollective.com/interviews/boyd-jarvis/
Producer, keyboardist and songwriter.

Producer, keyboardist and songwriter Boyd Jarvis grew up between Brooklyn, Boston and Harlem, and every stop added something to his sound.
The first record he bought with his own money was Crown Heights Affair's "Super Rod." The band lived on the corner of his block, he used to listen to them rehearse, and he even took "Super Rod" as his graffiti tag.
In Boston's Roxbury, radio stations like WILD played deep Black music, from the Isley Brothers to Gil Scott-Heron. At the Harriet Tubman House, a community center in a four-story brownstone, he would climb to the top floor and listen to musicians rehearse. That's where he fell in love with fusion jazz, and with heroes like George Duke, Chick Corea, Stanley Clarke and Herbie Hancock.
Back in New York, he started spinning and buying records around 1976. His first professional record grew out of an instrumental and became "The Music Got Me," released by Prelude after he and his partner were already playing their instrumentals on WBLS.

Quotes:
- "To us it was all just funky." — Boyd Jarvis
- "That was our music." — Boyd Jarvis

Playlist: Crown Heights Affair – "Super Rod"; Sly and the Family Stone; Isley Brothers; Gil Scott-Heron; George Duke; Herbie Hancock
